meta.title: Modern AI & Transformation of Clinical, Operational & Research Infrastructure in Pathology

glossary.definition: A Yale-built, web-based quality-control application that compares a draft pathology report against the patient's record — requisition, clinical notes, operative report, imaging, prior reports — before the report is finalized, and shows the pathologist what disagrees. In clinical use since March 2025, run by the pathologist before sign-out; since September 2026 Starling can also ask for a review at finalize, in a pilot.
The Yale-built pathology platform in which pathologists work up and finalize cases. Since September 2026 it can ask Dialogue to review a report at finalize (“Review with AI”), in a pilot.

A Yale specimen-custody application built in 2023–2025 after two spreadsheet-based tracking systems failed. Manifests travel with specimens between the operating room and the laboratory and stay open until the receiving party acknowledges them. Large language models helped write its specifications and code; none of them runs inside it.

Interactive Biomedical Inquiry System — an open-source search engine for anatomic pathology that turns a question in plain words into a search (a Lucene query) over structured and free-text case data, shows its interpretation and confidence, and waits for approval before executing. Built on synthetic data outside the institution.

An open-source generator of synthetic patient and staff records that sound like records, belong to nobody, and — in stress mode — include the values that break pipelines: empty strings, injection strings, diacritics, improbable dates. It establishes that a pipeline survives contact with data, not that the data are clinically plausible.

A keyboard-driven manual differential white-cell counter (also called the MDC), open source, with a full medical-device-style quality system: 71 user requirements, 207 system requirements, 56 hazards, 1,172 tests, and an append-only log of every claim that stopped being true.
Manual Differential Counter — the working name of WBC ΔΣ in the residents' lectures and in the repository's own code.

A Yale application (2012–) that links the operating room and the frozen-section area: the frozen-section diagnosis is entered once, sent to the OR for acknowledgment, and uploaded automatically to the laboratory information system.

Pathology Orders in Transit — a Yale application (2018–) that links the LIS with the EHR's ordering modules and tracks a specimen from the moment of biopsy or resection to its arrival in the laboratory.

Repetitive Task Scheduling Engine — Yale's workflow-orchestration engine (2007–), running the department's scheduled jobs: targeted reminders, clinical alerts, rare-event detection, system checks and data-integrity verification.
Rapidly Evolving Agile Laboratory Modules — the umbrella name for the assembly of small applications, on premises and in the cloud, that Yale Pathology Informatics runs alongside the commercial LIS.
Laboratory information system — the laboratory’s system of record for specimens, slides, results and reports, from accessioning to sign-out.

Electronic health record — the hospital’s record of a patient’s care over time: encounters, orders, notes, results, imaging and other documents. The pathology report is filed into it, and it is one of the sources a coherence check reads.
Health Level Seven — the messaging standard through which laboratory and hospital systems exchange orders, results and documents.
The form that accompanies a specimen to the laboratory: who the patient is, what was taken, from where, and why. One of the documents a coherence check reads.
The surgeon's or proceduralist's account of what was done and what was seen. It may be dictated but unsigned when the specimen arrives.
Left or right. A laterality error in a report is one of the most consequential and most mechanical mistakes a document check can catch.

A pathology report corrected after release. Yale's 2014 study of 60 amended reports found that in seven cases the ordering and treating physicians differed, and the amendment reached the treating physician's chart in only one.

A disagreement between two statements about the same patient, specimen or finding. Which discrepancies matter — and which are only differences in wording — is a pathology question, not a programming detail.
An intraoperative consultation in which tissue is frozen, cut and read within minutes so the surgeon can act. The permanent section, read days later, is the reference against which it is scored.

Frozen-section quality assurance — the scoring of each frozen-section diagnosis against the permanent diagnosis, with the source of any discrepancy categorized and the discrepancy documented in the final report.
A required step the system will not let you skip. In the frozen-section QA program, scoring at sign-out became a hard stop six months after go-live.
Who has a specimen, where it is, and who has acknowledged receiving it — a chain that a spreadsheet can describe but cannot enforce.

A list of the specimens or slides traveling together from one place to another, created where they leave and closed only when the receiving party acknowledges them. The word is borrowed from shipping.
The transfer of a specimen, a case or a task from one person or place to another. In most laboratory systems it is implicit; in an orchestrated one it has a state, an owner and a deadline.
A positive confirmation by the receiving party that something arrived. The difference between a message delivered and a step completed.
A layer that knows what must happen next in a workflow, who must do it, by when, and what to do when nobody does. Distinct from exchanging messages between systems.
Whether systems can coordinate the next step in the work, not merely exchange information about it. Asked as a practical question: who acts, who confirms, what happens when nobody does.
A model in which an object is always in exactly one named state and moves between states only through defined transitions. A handoff that must be acknowledged is a state machine with three states.
The part of a system whose behavior is fixed by its rules and tests rather than by a model's judgment. The place where routine operational decisions should live.

A model trained on very large amounts of text that can read, compare, summarize, translate and generate language and code. Inside an application it proposes; in a build it helps construct. The two uses need different evidence.

Software development in which an AI assistant plans, writes, runs and tests code toward a stated goal, in a conversation that keeps no memory once it ends. Capable and thorough; which is why the quality controls have to be written down and run.
User requirements specification — what must be true, stated by the people who will use the system, each with a clinical rationale. The document only a domain expert can write.
System requirements specification — testable statements of system behavior derived from the user requirements.
Failure mode and effects analysis — a risk analysis that lists each way a system could fail, scores severity, occurrence and detectability, and names the control for each.
A table linking every requirement to the tests that verify it and the hazards it mitigates, in both directions. Only meaningful when it is generated from the artifacts rather than typed.

The international standard that defines the software development life-cycle requirements for medical-device software. It emphasizes safe and reliable software through risk management, documentation and systematic processes to ensure patient safety. Software is classed A, B or C by the harm a failure could cause.
The controlled set of documents that records how a device was designed, verified and changed. For WBC ΔΣ it is public and inspectable.

Evidence that the software does what its written requirements say, usually from tests that run the software as it is installed. A test that runs a copy of the logic instead of the program itself verifies nothing about the program.
Evidence that the software serves its intended use in practice: a measured interval, a documented rate, a change in the work. Distinct from verification.
A discipline for new tests: remove the fix, and the test must fail with the original symptom. Twice in the counter's history it found the test wrong before it found the code wrong.

The decay of a repository's statements about itself: documents, comments, procedures and counts that stop agreeing with the code and with each other. Acute when capable but stateless sessions do the work.
A quality management system whose controls run in the build — generated counts, consistency gates, provenance-stamped evidence — so that drift fails the build instead of waiting for a reviewer.
The rule that closing anything — a hazard, a gap, an open item — means touching everything that speaks about it. Closing without sweeping is how most drift incidents happened.
Records generated to resemble real ones without describing any real person. They let systems be built and tested outside the institution’s network, with no patient data involved.
Xenonym's mode that deliberately generates the values that break systems — empty, oversized, injected, accented, improbable — so the pipeline meets them in a test rather than in production.

The declared shape of a record: which fields exist and what kind of value each holds. A record that satisfies the schema has the right shape; whether its contents are plausible is a separate question.
The query language beneath Elasticsearch: fields, boolean operators, wildcards and ranges. IBIS translates a natural-language question into it and shows the result before running it.
Asking a database a question in ordinary language. The useful part is not the fluency of the answer but the search it generates, which you can read before it runs.
The set of patients, specimens or reports that meets a definition. Which of the three units is being counted decides the number.
In IBIS, the step that shows the interpretation, the confidence, the terms it recognized and the generated query, and waits for the user to approve before anything executes.
The small, accountable group between IT and the clinicians that hears a question, sharpens it, builds inside the institution’s own network, verifies, and owns the software afterward.
Something important, technically attainable, and absent from the vendor system — Gershkovich and Sinard, 2015. The place where custom infrastructure begins.
Protected health information — health information that identifies a patient. In the systems in this talk it never leaves the institution’s network; IBIS and the counter were built on synthetic data.
The defined purpose a tool is validated for. A coherence check validated for laterality and site is not thereby validated for diagnosis.

The idea behind the earlier lectures in this series: spoken intent can be turned into running, tested software — a form, a page, a visualization, a prototype — so the domain expert can say what a tool should do and watch it appear. This talk is about what that does to clinical practice.

James Reason’s picture of how systems fail: each defensive layer is a slice with holes that open, close and move; no single hole causes harm, and harm needs the holes in several layers to line up. BMJ 2000;320:768–770.

The Joint Commission’s term for a patient-safety event that results in death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm. Wrong-surgery events were the second most frequently reported category in 2024, after falls.
A serious, largely preventable adverse event that should not occur if available safeguards are in place; wrong-site, wrong-patient and wrong-procedure surgery are the standard examples.

An operation on the wrong side, the wrong level or the wrong structure. In the Joint Commission’s review of 2024, 68% of wrong-surgery events were wrong-site, and incorrect laterality was cited in over half of those.

Whether a tissue specimen actually came from the patient whose name it carries. Occult provenance complications, switching and contamination, are measured by DNA comparison and were found in roughly one percent of prostate biopsies in a 2013 study.

Two forms of a claim about the future. A prophecy names an outcome and a date and gives no mechanism, so it cannot be checked until the date passes. A specification describes what a system would have to do, so it can be read backward from its conclusion and checked step by step — and can be wrong in its particulars and still useful.

The two defect types that matter most in the Meier taxonomy of amended reports. A misinterpretation changes the diagnosis; a misidentification attaches a correct diagnosis to the wrong patient, specimen or site. With specimen defects and report defects they are the four categories of the CAP Q-Probes benchmark on the opening slide.

The College of American Pathologists’ voluntary, multi-institution quality benchmarking studies. The 2014 study of 73 institutions supplies the amended-report split on the opening slide; the 1998 study of 359 laboratories is the older benchmark.

The tendency to accept a machine’s output in place of one’s own check — Mukherjee’s parent whose child has spell-check and never learns to spell. The reason a coherence check asks the pathologist to decide and records the decision.

An FDA-authorized AI detection assist for prostate needle biopsies, for adjunctive use: it reads the slide image, and the pathologist makes the diagnosis. In use at Yale as a quality check on prostate biopsies since 2026.

The one new service in Yale’s Paige Prostate integration: it registers cases with Paige, receives slide-by-slide completion notices, and reports status to the pathologist’s worklist. Written with AI assistance under a medical-device software process; it contains no model.
The current version of Yale’s Repetitive Task Scheduling Engine; it hosts the scheduled job that selects eligible prostate biopsies and checks their identifiers before anything is sent.

A conversation with an AI assistant in which it writes code, tests and documents toward a stated goal. When the conversation ends the assistant remembers nothing of it, so what a system must do has to live in written requirements and tests, not in the session.

An AI program, usually a large language model, that a person works with in conversation: it drafts, proposes and explains, and the person decides. In this talk it helps build systems; it runs inside only one of them.
An AI that returns a result and nothing more. The first of the three meanings of “AI” in this talk: the kind that can replace a task, and the only kind the 2016 prediction imagined.
A system you can talk with: it proposes an answer, shows how it reached it, and lets you judge, correct or dismiss it. The second of the three meanings of “AI” in this talk; Dialogue is one.

An AI that helps build the system itself: it turns a stated intention into requirements, code, tests and documents. The third meaning of “AI” in this talk. What makes it safe is that the result is ordinary software, which can be tested.

AI that produces new text, code or images from a prompt, usually a large language model. The model inside Dialogue and the assistant that helped build the other systems are both of this kind; the difference is where they sit.

Building a dependable system around a model: correct inputs and identity, the workflow, usable outputs, validation, monitoring, fallback and ownership. The model is the engine; AI engineering builds the vehicle (Software Engineering Institute, 2021).

Using AI assistants to build ordinary software faster: the specification, the code, the tests and the documents drafted in conversation, then reviewed and tested. The approach behind every system in this talk that has no model inside it.

Licklider’s 1960 vision of people and computers working as partners, the computer helping to formulate the problem and not only to solve one already stated. He listed what was missing before it could happen, which is what made the vision useful.

The future cost of shortcuts taken in software today. Sculley and colleagues (2015) showed that in a machine-learning system most of it accumulates not in the model but in everything around it: data, configuration, monitoring, serving.

A search written in a form a database can execute: which fields, which values, combined how. IBIS turns a question in plain words into one and shows it before running it, so the search can be read, checked and repeated.
In Starling, the action that closes a report and sends it for sign-out: the last moment at which the record is still correctable, and the point at which Starling can ask Dialogue for a review.
A comparison of a draft report against the other documents about the same patient — requisition, notes, operative report, imaging, prior reports — to find where they disagree. What Dialogue does.

A sequence of questions put to a language model in order, each building on the last. In Dialogue a review is such a chain; it is edited by an administrator on screen and versioned, so every result records which version ran.
A test case whose correct result is known in advance. Dialogue runs such cases through a check before pathologists see its flags; a check that gets them wrong does not go live.
One saved, described set of changes to a program’s code. Counting commits counts activity, not value.
A set of code changes reviewed by someone else and accepted into the program (a merged pull request). The unit of reviewed work on a department’s code server.

The routine parts of a program that every application needs before its particular logic can be written: connections, screens, data storage, the frame of the tests. The part an AI assistant now writes first.
Statements of what the system must do and must never do, each written so that a test can show whether it is true. In this talk, the sentences only the pathologist can write.
A written description of what a system should do, what it must never do, and what would show it works. The page this talk asks every pathologist to write.
What a person would need to see to accept that the system works: a measured interval, a rate, a test that fails when the behavior is removed. Stated before the system is built.
The program as it is actually installed and used, as opposed to a copy or a re-implementation written for a test. A test is worth something only if it runs the shipped code.
Tests that pass without running the program they claim to test: they verify a copy of the logic, or check that the code contains certain words. A green build with nothing behind it.

Unit tests call one piece of the program directly; behavior tests drive the whole application as a user would; system tests run the installed application in real browsers. The counter has all three, and none of them runs a copy.
A test built from inputs chosen to break the system: empty fields, impossible dates, text that looks like a command. Xenonym generates such records on purpose.
A short number computed from a file’s contents. If the file arrives with a different checksum, it was changed on the way.
The message a vendor sends back when it has finished reading a slide. The Paige integration waits for it, checks it, and only then shows the case as ready.

In a hazard analysis, a score for each way a system could fail: how severe the harm would be, how often it could happen, and how hard it would be to notice, multiplied together. Controls lower the score by making a failure rarer or easier to notice; they cannot make it less severe.

The international standard for risk management of medical devices: identify each hazard, estimate and evaluate its risk, control it, and keep the record. The Paige integration’s hazard analysis follows it.

Five claims a system can make, each needing a different kind of evidence: the data has the right shape; the code passes a test; each requirement is verified; it changed the work in practice; patients did better. Saying which rung you are on is the honest way to describe any system.
Design history file; see that entry.
Requirements traceability matrix; see traceability matrix.
Design change record — the counter’s numbered record of a change, why it was made and what it touched. DCR-004 is the one that found that the tests executed nothing.
Large language model; see that entry.

slides.speakerNotes:
The promise for the hour. By one o'clock you will be able to do three things. Tell, in one sentence, which kind of AI someone is proposing to you, and what evidence it needs. Say, for one problem you have lived with, what a system should do, what it must never do, and what would convince you it works. And read a report the way these systems read it, before it leaves the department. None of that is programming. All of it is pathology. Pause two seconds.

slides.speakerNotes:
The opening argument, seven to eight minutes, and one sentence to hold: the most useful visions do not merely predict what machines will do; they help us specify what must be built so that people can do something better. Nine anchors on one line, in order, not to scale. Click. 1928, publish or perish: ask the room how old the phrase is; documented in Case 1928 and Wilson 1942, no first use and no inventor claimed. Producing a publication is not making knowledge usable. 1945, Bush, As We May Think: the Memex, a personal microfilm desk with annotations and associative trails; preserve the connections, not only the documents. Proposed, not built; a design vision, not a specification; it anticipated hypertext, not the Internet. 1960, Licklider, Man-Computer Symbiosis: help formulate problems, not merely solve preformulated ones; he listed the prerequisites, time-sharing, memory, languages, displays, networked centers. A vision becomes a research program when it says what is missing. Click. 1958 to 1972, ARPA, IPTO, the first ARPANET message on 29 October 1969, DARPA in 1972: working infrastructure was a collective accomplishment, not one paper becoming reality. 1983 and 1988, Tufte and Norman: can people understand what to do, can they inspect the evidence; these slides are an application of that, not a claim that Tufte invented them. 1989, Berners-Lee at CERN: linked information on the network that already existed; he invented the Web, not the Internet, and Bush belongs to the hypertext lineage, not a single causal chain. Click. 2015, Sculley and colleagues, hidden technical debt: a small machine-learning component surrounded by data collection, verification, serving, configuration, monitoring; the diagram is conceptual, not a measured share of cost. 2016 and 2017, CAMELYON16 in JAMA: some algorithms exceeded the pathologist panel in a simulated, time-constrained evaluation; the achievement was real, and the question is what it established: a task is not the whole profession, and an experimental result is not a clinical service. 2021, the SEI framework for AI engineering, human-centered, robust and secure, scalable; not the birth of systems engineering. Correct inputs and identity, workflow, usable outputs, validation, monitoring, fallback, ownership. AI may be the engine; our responsibility is to build the vehicle. Two guardrails as you speak: contrast unsupported inevitability with testable design proposals, not old visionaries against new researchers, since Bush and Licklider speculated too; and do not describe statistics, data science, data engineering and AI engineering as replacement professions. The transition: there are two roles for AI, AI inside the system and AI helping us build the system; the second changes how directly clinical expertise can shape the tools of pathology. Let me show you what that means.

takeaway.text: The most useful visions do not predict what machines will do. They specify what must be built so that people can do something better.

vizConfig.thesis: The prediction aimed at judgment, the hardest part, and missed the commonest errors: context. Software can catch those, and nobody had built it.

slides.speakerNotes:
THE OPENING, about three minutes, two clicks. Read the quote and let the hedge sit; it is on the slide because it is fair. (Mukherjee’s own line, “the algorithm can solve a case; it cannot build a case”, came off the slide on 22 October; say it if it helps, and say that building a case means assembling the record around the slide.) Attribution matters in this room: the lines are Hinton’s. Mukherjee carried them, and his own conclusion ran the other way, toward augmentation and the danger of automation bias. Do not argue with the person; argue with the form of the claim. A dated outcome with no mechanism cannot be read backward and checked step by step. Bush and Licklider were wrong in most of their particulars and still useful, because they described mechanisms. You would never give a patient a prognosis with a date and no mechanism. Click: ten years later. The most diagnostic radiology positions in five years and nearly all of them filled; 636 pathology positions; the Mayo Clinic went from about 260 radiologists to more than 400; and in May 2025 the author of the prediction told the Times he had been wrong on the timing, not the direction, and had spoken only about image analysis. Click: what actually sends a report back. In the 2014 Q-Probes benchmark, one amended report in seven changed the interpretation; the taxonomy paper puts the fraction between a quarter and three in ten. Either way, most amendments are identification, specimen and report defects: a side, a part, a sentence that belongs to another case. The prediction aimed at judgment, the hardest thing, and missed context, the most common. Judgment is scarce and the room knows it. Context is engineering, and nobody engineered it. That sentence is the talk. If you have split the department’s own amendments by the same taxonomy, put the department’s numbers here in place of the benchmark; it is the strongest slide you can show. Two places a hostile listener will stand: wrong-site surgery is mostly an operating-room process failure, so keep the pathology version narrow, the amendment that arrives after the surgery because the side on the report was wrong; and define the missing component by what Dialogue needed that the model did not supply: reading the case before sign-out, sitting at the right point in the workflow, and a record of what it caught.

NEXT → Here is what actually goes wrong: three cases, three documents each, and you will read them yourselves.  [cold-open-case]

takeaway.text: The 2016 prediction aimed at judgment. What sends a report back is mostly context: identification, specimen and report defects. Software can catch those errors, and until recently nobody had built it.
takeaway.comment: Prophecy against specification. The quarrel is with the form of the claim, not the person: a dated outcome with no mechanism cannot be read backward and checked step by step, and the hedge stays on the slide because it was fairly made. Everything this hour claims is stated as a mechanism — what it took to build, what it caught, what most places still lack — and carries no date. The 14.6% is the 2014 Q-Probes figure, the lowest of the three CAP studies: the 2008 taxonomy study puts misinterpretation at 23–29% of amended reports, and the 1998 Q-Probes 38.7% as a change of final diagnosis. Context is the majority in every one.

slides.speakerNotes: OPTIONAL, one minute. The anxiety you remember in the residents’ room was measured. Canada, 2018: one in six students who would have ranked radiology first would not, because of AI; nearly half of the first-choice students called it a source of anxiety. The United Kingdom a year later: 49% of 484 students less likely to consider radiology. The United States in 2020: one in six again. The prediction had a measurable cost years before it had a measurable benefit. Then the author’s own revision in 2025. No commentary needed; the four numbers do the work. Cut this slide first if the hour is tight. The 2025 quotation is as reported by AuntMinnie and The Decoder from Lohr’s Times piece of 14 May 2025; the Times text itself was not checked, so present it as reported.

takeaway.text: The prediction had a measurable cost years before it had a measurable benefit.
takeaway.comment: Three surveys of medical students, 2018 to 2020 — Gong (Canada), Sit (United Kingdom), Reeder and Lee (United States) — asked the same question and got the same answer: students who would have chosen radiology were turning away because of AI, one in six in Canada and the United States, nearly half less likely in the United Kingdom. The prediction did not have to be right to have an effect. It had to be heard by people choosing a specialty, and it was heard years before its author revised it.

THE CASES, right after the prediction: three cases, about four minutes. The prediction aimed at judgment; here is what actually goes wrong. Case 1: say nothing for ten seconds; let the room read; ask what does not agree. Someone finds the side. Click: the laterality lines turn crimson and an amber pair appears, three cores against three core samples. Ask which of the two they would act on; that is the first lesson, which contradictions matter is a pathology question. Click for the flag, click for the decision, which is the pathologist’s. Click for case 2 and ask the same question. The requisition says seventy; the report header says thirty; the clinical history, as histories do, gives no age or name. Someone will see the ages. Someone else will say Grade Group 2 at thirty. Both point the same way: the histology is not in doubt, the accession is. The case was accessioned to the wrong patient, and the cores belong to the seventy-year-old on the requisition. Verify identity and date of birth against registration before release, re-accession, and the right report goes out under the right name. Two things to notice: the header check is a comparison a machine can make, and the age check is the one that needs what a pathologist knows — and it is the second that makes you look twice at the first. Case 3: Part B was received, accessioned, and never reported, and the comment recommends mammographic correlation in a colon case. Two flags, one of them the error that amendments are made of. The closing line ties the three together: side, identity, completeness, and three wording differences that were not errors. All cases are synthetic; the banner says so. The breast case mirrors a real October 2025 catch at Yale. Close with one sentence of stakes, because the slide of public cases is hidden: these errors are not hypothetical. Long Island, 2007: two biopsies swapped at a reference lab, and a double mastectomy for a cancer that belonged to someone else. The histology was right; the record was wrong.

The claim, stated once, on the picture it sits on: two programs for AI in pathology, drawn on the same ten years. Above, AI engineering, the program the prediction belongs to: build the model that does the pathologist’s work. Its question is the usual one, can a computer recognize what we recognize. Click. Its horizon: five years, then maybe ten, and this month the generous version expires; in May 2025 Hinton said he had been wrong on the timing, not the direction. The date keeps moving. In this department the program has exactly one entry: a bought model, authorized, adjunctive, under clinical evaluation since May, with no results yet; the dashed line is the evaluation, still open. That is not a failure; it is what per-task evidence costs. Click. Below, engineering with AI: build the systems we already know we need. Its question is this hour’s: what happens when what we know becomes a system that works that way? Look at the empty years, then at the last three. The bars reach today: a custody system in use since 2023, Dialogue reading the record before sign-out since March 2025, an integration built in ten weeks and in use since May; and two more that exist, a research tool on synthetic data and a counter whose tests execute it. The figure is my own output, measured on our git server: ten to a hundred times per working day, at the same gates; one engineer, five weeks in, two to four times. Nothing built this way for seven years, then everything at once, because the cost collapsed. Click. The replacement is still a forecast; the systems are in use today. The immediate utility is the second program, and it is yours to direct. Hold the sentence: pathologists are becoming designers of how pathology works, because the cost of making a system behave the way we know it should has collapsed. I will say it three times, each time with a system behind it, and I will fence it: not everyone becomes a programmer, and we still need engineers.

slides.speakerNotes:
This is the intellectual tension of the hour, and the reason a grand-rounds audience is the right one. One sentence per row. The three cases are the ones the room read at the start; the second row is what the machine says about each: differs, differs, differs, flagged. It reads everything and says one of two things. Click: which of these matters is your call. Three cores against three core samples is not a discrepancy; left against right is. The ages differ: which one is the patient? Grade Group 2 at thirty is the tell, and that is the part a machine cannot supply. A received part with no diagnosis: an omission, or a decision not to report yet, and should the system proceed or stop and ask? These are substantive pathology questions. The programming is the easy part now. Click: once you say it, we can test for it. Each question is replaced by its answer written as a rule, and a rule is a known-answer case the chain is run against before a pathologist sees a flag. The rules on the slide are illustrations, phrased the way ours are; the list is never finished. Two more questions stay in the notes rather than on the slide: what the system actually had in front of it when it found no mismatch (an operative note signed after the review ran was not in the review, and no flag on it is not a clearance; the safety-boundary slide repeats this), and what you must see before you dismiss a flag, its sentence or the two lines it compared (the scrutiny layer shows the lines). If there is time, ask the room for a fourth column. There is always one, and it is usually better than mine.

takeaway.comment: The right-hand column is never finished, and every item on it is a judgment before it is a rule. Whether a Grade Group 2 adenocarcinoma at thirty is implausible or merely unusual, whether a missing part is an omission or a decision, whether a pasted sentence is a shortcut or an error — each is something only a pathologist can decide, and once written down it becomes a specification a system can be tested against.

cards.text: Specimens went missing between the operating room and pathology intake. Ad-hoc, Excel-based tracking failed twice: nothing enforced a consistent workflow, so custody had gaps.
A handoff is not complete merely because somebody entered a destination. The receiving party must acknowledge receipt, and an open handoff stays visible until they do.
A manifest, the list of what was sent, is created at the source, travels with the specimens, and stays open and visible to both ends until the receiver acknowledges it by name.
If a manifest is sent and not acknowledged within the time allowed, the system must alert the sender and the receiving location, and the test fails if it does not.

vizConfig.caption: Large language models contributed to the requirements, the architecture, the code and the security review of Hedgehog. None of them decides, while the system is in use, whether a specimen has arrived.

slides.speakerNotes:

The Hedgehog version has a transition called acknowledge and a guard under it. The audience does not need a code tour. It needs to see where the laboratory's knowledge changed the design — the requirement card, which I have labeled illustrative because it is my formulation of the rule, not a quotation from a document. Problem, requirement, behavior, test. That is the translation, and it is the same four cards for every system in this talk. No usage statistics are published; claim none. Second pass of the claim: we already knew that changing infrastructure changes practice; our own frozen-section QA, built into sign-out, took the time to scoring from seventy days to eight, published this year. What is new is how fast such infrastructure can be built, tested and revised.

NEXT → Second pass done. The third system is the opposite kind: a model inside the workflow, the kind the prediction was about, and we bought it.  [paige-prostate]

Frozen-section QA built into sign-out: scoring at the moment of sign-out, a reason required for disagreement, automated e-mail to the frozen-section pathologist, a weekly review module, and after six months a hard stop. These are infrastructure and workflow results. They are not evidence of an AI effect, and anyone who tells you otherwise about their own numbers is confusing two clocks. We already knew that changing infrastructure changes practice. The new question is how AI-assisted engineering changes our ability to build, test and revise it.

NEXT → Second pass done. The third system is the opposite kind: a model inside the workflow, the kind the prediction was about, and we bought it.  [paige-prostate]

takeaway.text: We already knew that changing infrastructure changes practice. The question now is how AI-assisted engineering changes our ability to build, test and revise it.
takeaway.comment: Gibson, Mutnick, Gershkovich and Sinard, Am J Clin Pathol 2025;163:794–802. The program is ordinary infrastructure, none of it AI: FSLink, a scoring module inside CoPath (agree, margin assurance, defer, disagree with a reason), an automated e-mail to the frozen-section pathologist, a weekly review module and a quarterly M&M conference. slides.speakerNotes: The interoperability argument, introduced as a practical question rather than as standards terminology. On the left, exchange: the LIS sends a message and everybody gets a copy. On the right, a layer that holds state — what must happen next, who must acknowledge, what to do when nobody does — and the systems that have been doing this at Yale for years: FSLink waiting for the OR to acknowledge a frozen-section diagnosis, POinT following an order in transit, Hedgehog holding custody open, RTSE running the reminders and rare-event detection. takeaway.text: Exchanging a message is not the same as coordinating the next step. The second is what the laboratory actually needs.
takeaway.comment: Gershkovich P. Wearing a fur coat in the summertime: should digital pathology redefine medical imaging? J Pathol Inform 2025;18:100450. A message tells the next system that something happened. Coordination tells the next person what to do about it, by when, and what happens if they do not — and keeps the record that they did. FSLink is the smallest example: a frozen-section diagnosis sent to the operating room waits for acknowledgment, and silence becomes an event rather than an absence. Standards describe the envelope; the laboratory’s problem is the contract.

slides.speakerNotes:
Two clicks. Hedgehog was AI helping build something with no model inside it. Here is the opposite: a model inside the workflow — the kind of AI the 2016 prediction was about — and we bought it. Ten weeks from vendor account to clinical use. As drawn, everything you see was already in use: the Portal pathologists work in, the scheduler that already runs other pathology jobs, the imaging systems, single sign-on, audit, the hospital network. One slot is empty. Click: the one new service, Bulldog Bridge — written with AI assistance under a medical-device software process, no model in it. It registers each case with Paige, hears when a slide has been read, and puts the status in the Portal. Strictly, the scheduler also gained a new job and the Portal a status and a launch button; the Bridge is the only new service. Most of the ten weeks went to regulated-software discipline (requirements, risk analysis, validation, procedures, traceability), not to code; the verification section picks that up. Click: one biopsy’s path, in order. One, eligible and identity checked. Two, registered with Paige first. Three, read in Paige’s cloud. Four, ready in the worklist, one click into Paige’s viewer, already signed in. The pathologist reads the slide and decides; the output is adjunctive and sign-out is never gated by it. If asked about failures: LIS unreachable, image missing, Paige silent, a notification that never arrives — logged with a reason, an administrator alerted, retried on the next cycle; no case is silently lost. Yale’s public account is the Yale Cancer Center article of 14 August 2026: the platform is a quality check, a bridge built by the informatics team carries the data, metrics are still being collected. The integration’s own risk analysis is not in the published deck; its point is: every risk it had to control is context — identity, timing, status, privacy — and not one is about whether the model reads the slide. Say it here, as the third pass of the claim and the opening returned.

takeaway.comment: If anything fails — the LIS unreachable, an image missing, Paige silent, a notification that never arrives — the case is logged with a reason, an administrator is alerted, and it is retried on the next cycle; no case is silently lost. The new service was written with AI assistance and has no model in it: both kinds of AI the talk separates, in one project.

slides.speakerNotes:
You have now seen both, and Paige was both at once: a model inside the workflow that someone else built, and an integration around it that AI helped us build and that has no model in it. On the left, a model runs inside the application: Dialogue reads, proposes, and a pathologist decides. Its outputs need evaluation appropriate to the task, which flags matter, which are noise, what it could not see. On the right, a model helped build the application and then left: the Paige integration has no model inside it. A biopsy is eligible or it is not, it was sent or it was not, a result came back or it did not, and nothing probabilistic decides any of that. The model it feeds is Paige’s, and that is the left kind. The integration still needs engineering review and validation, but it behaves predictably, and for the piece that moves patient slides to a vendor, predictable is the whole point. This is the one distinction I would ask you to keep, because it stops the word AI from becoming an explanation for everything that follows.

NEXT → Both kinds, kept separate. Now the research system, and this one is live.  [ibis-live]

takeaway.text: The goal is dependable functionality, not the maximum amount of AI in the workflow.
takeaway.comment: For the people who came to hear about AI, the counterintuitive version: some of the most valuable systems AI helps us build should behave predictably, with no model making their routine operational decisions. A model inside the application proposes and must be evaluated for what it misses; a model that helped build the application has left by the time it runs, and what remains is ordinary software that can be tested. Paige is both at once, and both halves are on this slide: the bought model is the left kind, the integration around it the right. The orchestration lecture called the second kind the deterministic kernel. Same idea, plainer words.

slides.speakerNotes:
The objection everything so far should provoke: you can build this quickly; how do you know it behaves correctly? I will answer with the smallest application I have. A manual differential counter — press a key, the count goes up. Seventy-one user requirements, two hundred and seven system requirements, fifty-six hazards, eleven hundred and seventy-two tests, one hundred percent traceability. Every artifact is in a public repository. It is simple on purpose. The safety envelope around it is the part worth studying — and the next two slides are about where that envelope failed before it held. Counts are the README’s generated qms:fact fields at v2.24.0 (23 Aug 2026). The residents’ lecture quoted 156 tests and 47 requirements; those were true in February 2026 and are superseded. Say so if a resident remembers.

NEXT → Here is the revealing failure, and it is mine.  [green-build]

takeaway.text: The counter is simple on purpose. The requirements, hazards and tests around it are the part worth studying, including where they failed.
takeaway.comment: The counts are the counter’s own, generated from its quality-management records at version 2.24.0 (23 August 2026) rather than typed, because typed counts drifted. They have grown since this material was first shown in February 2026, when there were 156 tests and 47 requirements. An application this simple exists to make the envelope around it legible: requirements with a clinical rationale, hazards traced to controls, tests that execute the shipped code, and a public record of where all of that failed first.

slides.speakerNotes:
Here is the revealing failure, and it is mine. The v2.0 baseline: three hundred and seventy-nine tests, one hundred percent passing, every one of these green squares. Click. Zero of them executed the application. Half re-implemented the algorithms inside the test file and verified the copy; the rest checked that the source code contained certain strings. Click again. Fourteen real defects sat behind that green build: export buttons wired to nothing, percentages that never summed to a hundred, user input reaching a clinical report unescaped, formula injection in the CSV export. The suite that certified the build could not have caught any of them. Click once more. On the right, what it took: three layers that execute the shipped code, in three browsers, and two rules — no layer verifies a copy, and every new test is revert-checked. A system that passes a test is not the same as a system whose tests execute it. This is the failure mode that AI-assisted development makes cheap, and it is why the quality system has to be code, not prose. One entry from the counter’s own drift log, which used to be a slide: the operating procedure told the technologist to press A for blasts; the shipped keyboard layout had A as monocytes. Nobody wrote a false sentence; the layout changed and the procedure was not swept. Fifty-two such drifts are logged, forty-two now prevented by a check that fails the build. That is what “the executable quality system remembers” means on the safety-boundary slide and in the fifth takeaway. If challenged on 379: it is from DCR-004 §1; TR-001’s comparison table records 191 at the same baseline. The point survives either number.

NEXT → So which claim is each of these systems entitled to make? Five claims, five kinds of evidence.  [claims-ladder]

takeaway.comment: The 379 figure is from the project’s own change record (DCR-004); a later technical report counts 191 tests at the same baseline. The argument survives either number: none of them executed the application. A green build is a statement about the tests, not about the software. It becomes a statement about the software only when the tests are shown to reach it — which is what the two rules on the right enforce, and what revert-checking proved twice by finding the test wrong before the code.

slides.speakerNotes: Fifty-two incidents in which the repository asserted something that had stopped being true, logged append-only, forty-two now prevented by a check that fails the build. The headline: the operating procedure said press A for blasts; the shipped layout had A as monocytes. Nobody wrote a false sentence. The layout changed, correctly, with tests, and the procedure was not swept. In a hematology laboratory the distance between blasts and monocytes is the distance between leukemia and a normal marrow. The taxonomy: counts kept by hand, two writers for one fact, closures not swept, versions advanced in one place, evidence without provenance — and one row, in crimson, still unguarded. What fixed it was not a better model. The quality system had existed from the start, as prose, and caught nothing. It started catching things when it became code.

takeaway.text: The quality system caught nothing while it was prose. It started catching things when it became code that fails the build.
takeaway.comment: The transferable lesson: treat AI sessions as capable staff who rotate every conversation, and give them what regulated laboratories learned to give rotating staff — document control, change records, a closure checklist, and verification that depends on nobody’s memory. Nothing here was careless; each session answered the question it was asked and never asked what else says this. None of it requires a medical context, and all of it is cheaper than the incident it prevents.

slides.title: Xenonym — The Records That Break Pipelines
slides.subtitle: Live at xenonym.openpathology.org — synthetic test cases in a realistic mode and a stress mode
slides.speakerNotes: Sixty seconds. Every system in this talk was built on synthetic data outside the institution. Xenonym is where the test cases come from: names that sound like names and belong to nobody, and in stress mode, the ones that break pipelines — the empty string, the injection string, the diacritics, the improbable date. Say what it establishes and what it does not. A schema-conforming synthetic record proves your pipeline accepts the shape. It does not prove the record is clinically plausible, and it is not a privacy guarantee. The next harness to build is the one Dialogue needs: records that are individually valid and mutually inconsistent. Xenonym has no cross-record consistency feature; do not claim one.

takeaway.text: Schema-conforming synthetic data establish neither clinical validity nor a privacy guarantee. They establish that your pipeline survives contact with data.
takeaway.comment: Xenonym generates records that are each valid against the schema, including the ones that break pipelines; it has no notion of consistency between records. The test set Dialogue actually needs — records individually valid and mutually inconsistent, a requisition that says left and a note that says right — is the obvious next tool, and it is exactly the kind of supplementary infrastructure that has become affordable to build.

slides.speakerNotes:
Five claims, five kinds of evidence. A record that satisfies a schema — Xenonym. A system that passes a test — the counter, and only because the tests execute the shipped code. A verified requirement — the traceability matrix, generated. A capability validated in use — the frozen-section program, measured over nearly three thousand frozen sections; Dialogue is partly here: its use is measured, and what it changed is the pathologists’ own account, not a measurement. And the fifth rung, patients did better, which is empty for all of them and stays empty until someone measures it. The conclusion is not that AI is unreliable so be careful. It is that faster construction makes explicit requirements, expert review and good tests more valuable, not less — and this ladder is how you say which claim you are making.

slides.speakerNotes:
Four systems, four sentences, and in every case the sentence the software could not have written for itself. What differs is where it enters. Paige: at the door, which cases a bought model may see. Unsigned prostate needle biopsies on a validated stain protocol; nothing else, an unknown stain included. Dialogue: inside the judgment, what counts as a difference. Ignore wording that does not change the diagnosis; raise side, site, identity and specimen. IBIS: before anything acts, what must be shown. The interpretation and the query, then approval, and the unit of the result stated rather than assumed. The counter: in the report, what it must carry. A count below the target is never blocked, and the report says the count, the target and the interval that count supports. Requirements are patient safety made explicit, and writing them is the part of this work that belongs to the people in this room. Provenance, if asked: the counter’s sentence is from its published requirements; the IBIS sentence from its README; the Paige sentence is the integration’s inclusion rule; the Dialogue sentence is my paraphrase of how the tool is described, not a quotation from a written requirement. If you have the real sentence, use it.

slides.speakerNotes:
Two models I reject, struck through on either side. Everyone becomes a programmer: unsupported tools, verification theater, drift, security left to good intentions. We no longer need engineering: untestable requirements, a model that proposes mistaken for a system that is accountable, nobody owning the artifact after the demo. The one in the middle is the one that has worked here for twenty years and now works faster: pathologists contribute the intended behavior, the meaningful exceptions and the acceptance criteria; an accountable team turns those into supported infrastructure. The loop at the bottom is the whole talk: intent, specification, build, test, use, revised intent. If the department chair is in the room, this is the slide to pause on.

The columns arrive one click at a time; read both aloud, because the non-negotiables matter as much as the capabilities. Left, what these systems let AI do: construct, propose, translate, generate, draft. Right, what none of them lets it do: decide, see patient data outside the institution, change data silently, go into use unverified, and the fifth, which this talk adds to the earlier lectures’ list: hold the requirements. A session forgets; the requirements and the tests that enforce them live outside it. A question to open the discussion:
“What is the one recurring problem you have accepted because changing the software seemed harder than living with it?”

And the three that turn it into infrastructure:
“What should the system do? What must it never do? What evidence would convince you that it works?”
slides.speakerNotes:
About sixty seconds, before opening questions. The published deck lists no names; say them. The history: the laboratory system was built largely here, under a license that gave Yale the source code and the right to build on it, which is why everything in this talk could be built on software we already had; the chair made this a section in 2019 and let us hire; the mentor who built the informatics program from the beginning gave me the chance to do this work, and the original vision was his and the people who worked with him: automate what they did by hand and free them from the tedious part. The engineering in this talk was done with the informatics team; none of it runs without clinical systems management, servers and databases, the help desk and support, and the laboratory’s management, who bring its priorities into ours. Many more than one slide can name, across the department, the laboratory and the health system: ten weeks for Paige took all of them.

vizConfig.title: What to take with you.
vizConfig.subtitle: Five things, and one page to write. Click.

items.claim: Pathologists are becoming designers of how pathology works.
items.gloss: The 2016 prediction aimed at diagnosis and missed the record around it. What stood between knowing what should happen and making it happen was the cost of implementation, and that cost has collapsed.

items.claim: Two kinds of AI: one proposes, one helps build.
items.gloss: Inside the application, a model proposes and needs task-appropriate evaluation. Helping build the application, no model remains in the finished system, which usually should behave predictably.

items.claim: A correct diagnosis is not a coherent clinical record.
items.gloss: Dialogue checks that the draft report agrees with the rest of the record. Which contradictions matter is a pathology question.

items.claim: Infrastructure changes practice; say what the evidence is.
items.gloss: Seventy days to eight came from a workflow change, not from a model. AI changes how fast such infrastructure can be built, tested and revised.

items.claim: Faster construction makes requirements, review and tests more valuable, not less.
items.gloss: A quality system protects no one until it is executable. Tests that pass but execute nothing are the failure mode AI makes cheap.

challenge.label: Your challenge
challenge.text: Pick one recurring problem you have accepted because changing the software seemed harder than living with it. Write the page: what the system should do, what it must never do, what evidence would convince you that it works. Bring it to the people who can build it.

slides.speakerNotes: Five things, read in order, each with one line of why; the glosses arrive on the first click. One, pathologists are becoming designers of how pathology works, because the cost of implementation collapsed. Two, two kinds of AI, kept separate. Three, a correct diagnosis is not a coherent record, and which contradictions matter is yours to say. Four, infrastructure changes practice; the seventy days to eight was a workflow result. Five, faster construction makes the requirements, the review and the tests more valuable, and a quality system protects no one until it executes. The last click is the ask: one problem, one page, brought to the people who can build it. This slide stays up through the questions. The first question is mine: what is the one recurring problem you have accepted because changing the software seemed harder than living with it? Then wait; do not say thank you.
